title: Distributed Rate Limiter: Complete Architecture
description: Design a distributed, low-latency API rate limiter supporting Token Bucket, Sliding Window Counter, Redis atomic Lua scripts, and multi-region sync.

data.text: Design a high-throughput, distributed rate limiter to safeguard microservices and public APIs from denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, brute-force attempts, web scrapers, and resource exhaustion. The rate limiter inspects incoming requests at the API Gateway layer, evaluates usage quotas against configured rules in under 1 millisecond at P99, and returns standard HTTP 429 Too Many Requests headers when quotas are exceeded — scaling horizontally to handle over 1 million requests per second.

terms.definition: Tokens are added to a bucket at a fixed rate `r` up to capacity `b`. Each request consumes 1 token. Allows controlled traffic bursts up to bucket capacity.
A hybrid memory-efficient algorithm combining previous and current window counts with a time-weighting factor to prevent boundary burst spikes in O(1) memory.
Standard status code accompanied by `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, `X-RateLimit-Reset`, and `Retry-After` headers.
Executing rate check and token decrement commands inside a single atomic Redis script to eliminate read-modify-write race conditions.
Local in-process LRU cache on the API gateway (L1) absorbs 80% of checks for non-violating keys, offloading the central Redis Cluster (L2).

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Multi-Algorithm Support: Token Bucket, Sliding Window Counter, and Fixed Window
Configurable Rate Limiting Keys: By User ID, API Key, Client IP address, or Composite (UserID + Endpoint)
Tiered Quotas: Dynamic limits per tier (e.g. Free: 60 req/min, Pro: 1,000 req/min, Internal: Unlimited)
Dynamic Rule Configuration: Update rate-limit policies in under 5 seconds without restarting gateway nodes
Allowlist & Bypass Rules: Exempt health check probes, internal service mesh calls, and VIP partner tokens

data.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items: Ultra-Low Latency: <1ms P99 decision latency added to the API request path
High Throughput: Handle 1,000,000+ rate limit evaluations per second
High Availability: Rate limiter failure must gracefully fail-open (never block valid traffic if limiter goes down)
Accuracy: Strict prevention of race conditions under concurrent requests from the same user across multiple servers
Distributed Multi-Region Scale: Synchronize quotas across geographically separated data centers

data.text: The rate limiter operates as an inline filter within the API Gateway (Envoy / Kong). It uses a local L1 in-memory cache for ultra-fast checks and a centralized Redis Cluster (L2) with atomic Lua scripts for distributed consistency.

data.text: To avoid concurrency race conditions where two simultaneous requests see the same token balance, the token refill and decrement logic executes inside a single atomic Redis Lua script.

data.caption: Rate limit evaluation sequence: Redis atomic Lua script execution with token replenishment calculation

1. Calculate tokens generated since last_refill_time
2. tokens = min(capacity, current_tokens + delta_tokens)
3. if tokens >= 1 then tokens-- and return (1, tokens)

faqs.question: Why use Redis Lua scripting instead of plain GET and SET commands?
faqs.answer: In a distributed system, two gateway nodes might concurrently read `tokens = 1`. Both subtract 1 and write back `tokens = 0`, allowing 2 requests instead of 1 (the Classic Race Condition). Redis Lua scripts run atomically in a single execution thread, ensuring no other operation can read or modify the token counter between the calculation and decrement.

faqs.question: What is the Fail-Open vs Fail-Closed philosophy in rate limiting?
faqs.answer: If the rate limiter or Redis cluster crashes, should you block all traffic (Fail-Closed) or allow all traffic through (Fail-Open)? For public customer APIs, always Fail-Open: it is better to risk overloading backend services than to guarantee a 100% outage for all legitimate users. For sensitive authentication endpoints (e.g. `/login` password brute-force protection), Fail-Closed is preferred for security.

faqs.question: How do you handle multi-region active-active synchronization without cross-datacenter latency?
faqs.answer: Synchronizing every token decrement across US, EU, and Asia data centers adds 150ms+ cross-continental latency to every API call. Solution: Partition the global quota across regions (e.g. US gets 50%, EU gets 30%, APAC gets 20% of the total limit), or run local token buckets with asynchronous background batch synchronization (gRPC/CRDTs) to sync consumption rates every 1-2 seconds.

faqs.question: How does the Sliding Window Counter algorithm calculate request allowance in O(1) memory?
faqs.answer: If a 1-minute window allows 100 requests, and the current time is 30% into the current window: `Requests in current window + (Requests in previous window * (1 - 0.30))`. This takes only two integers in memory while smoothing out boundary spikes with minimal approximation error.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Token Bucket allows controlled traffic bursts while enforcing strict long-term rate averages
Redis Lua scripts execute token calculation and consumption atomically, eliminating race conditions
Two-tier caching (in-process L1 on gateway + Redis Cluster L2) achieves sub-1ms decision latency
Fail-Open design ensures rate limiter infrastructure issues never cause complete public API outages
Multi-region setups partition quotas locally or use async batch syncing to avoid cross-region latency
data.takeaway: Distributed rate limiters combine in-memory Lua scripts with multi-tier caching at the API gateway layer to enforce granular security and usage policies with negligible latency overhead.
